course.title: Championing Women in Leadership - Climbing With Confidence

items.caption: Click play to hear the quote above.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
Now it’s time to take a look at some special areas of growth or opportunity for female leaders. We just outlined several of the challenges facing women in the workplace, so don’t let them take you by surprise! As Pat would say, knowing the opposition you are going to face in any situation never hurts. Rather, take things in stride, and learn how to navigate the workplace as it is, even as we all strive for improvement

This is important because when attempting to understand some of the hurdles facing women in leadership, many women get frustrated and simply give up. This may come in the form of career changes, opting out of the workforce, or simply quiet quitting.     

A key aspect to thriving in corporate leadership, for both men and women, but especially for women, is attitude. As mentioned in previous lessons, historically, women have lower levels of confidence based on the additional challenges they may face. And the key to boosting that confidence to a healthy level is attitude.

items.heading: Embrace Challenges as Opportunities
items.paragraph: To start, attitude involves viewing challenges not as insurmountable obstacles but as opportunities. Instead of shying away from difficulties, learn to embrace them with curiosity. Setbacks are a natural part of any career and can be viewed as stepping stones rather than stumbling blocks. By reframing challenges as chances to grow, as a woman, you can approach your career with a fresh sense of professionalism and optimism.

items.title: CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: The foundation of a positive attitude also begins with adopting a growth mindset. What do we mean by that? A growth mindset is the belief that abilities or intelligence can be developed through hard work. It’s understanding that our careers aren’t a byproduct of our circumstances or predetermined by external factors, but instead depends on our willingness to be challenged and grow. Some individuals may have to work harder to have a growth mindset in certain circumstances than others, but growth at its core is a resource available to everyone.

Pat firmly believed in a growth mindset, so much so that it was a prerequisite of everyone who played under her leadership. She famously said:

"How can you grow, if you never change? Without changing something almost every year, Tennessee never would have won five national championships…And without accepting some pretty dramatic changes in my own life, I wouldn’t be the head coach of the Lady Vols."

"There is nothing wrong with personal or professional growth, as long as you are strong in who you are and don’t lose sight of where you came from. Self-improvement doesn’t mean abandoning your old identity…Today, if someone tells me I’ve changed, I take it as a compliment. The plain fact is, without change, the game of women’s basketball would never have grown, nor I with it."

items.heading: So what does a "growth mindset" involve? Click on the icons to expand & view.

items.title: Viewing Setbacks as Learning Experiences
items.description: As mentioned, setbacks are an inevitable part of any journey, but the key lies in how you respond to them. Instead of dwelling on failures, leaders with a growth mindset see setbacks as valuable experiences. Analyze what went wrong, extract lessons, and use the newfound knowledge to pivot and move forward. You can’t grow if you’re not learning, even if that learning sometimes manifests itself as mistakes.

items.title: Listening to Criticism
items.description:
Constructive criticism is one of the most valuable tools for personal growth. The key is knowing how to seek it out and learn from it. Successful women leaders have mastered both. Instead of seeing feedback as a personal attack, strong women leaders view it as an opportunity to refine their skills. They have learned not to run from or avoid criticism, and know when it has helpful intentions behind it.

 

“The older I get, the more flexible I’d like to be,” Pat said. “Change is a force of nature; the truth is that nothing, good or bad, lasts forever. There will be setbacks, injuries, and adverse circumstances, and the person who deals best with them will win out.”

items.title: Setting Goals Regularly and Adapting
items.description: One fundamental part of any career is setting career-related goals. Setting goals is essential for growth, but a growth mindset also requires flexibility when going after those goals. This means regularly examining your objectives and taking into account new information and changing circumstances. Think of it as a game plan that has to be continually re-evaluated at the end of each season. Visualize yourself achieving your career goals and imagine the steps it takes to get there.

items.title: Surrounding Yourself With a Growth-Minded Community
items.description: It’s no secret that the company we keep plays a huge role in shaping our mindset. Surround yourself with individuals who share a growth mindset and encourage personal development. Engage in positive, growth-minded conversations and avoid relationships built on negativity.

items.title: Continuous Learning
items.description: The most obvious part of a growth mindset is continuous learning and skill development. The professional landscape is constantly changing, and staying ahead requires continual effort. Seek opportunities to enhance your skills, whether through formal education, workshops, or on-the-job training. Embrace a love of lifelong learning, new technologies, and industry trends. This can include formal education like conferences, workshops or online courses, or informal learning like reading and networking.

items.title: Committing to an Attitude of Resilience
items.description: Women are historically resilient, and the workplace is no exception. Men and women both have to be resilient at work, but often in different ways. Make it your mission to have an attitude of resilience in your career.  This includes positive self-talk, an attitude of gratefulness, and the willingness to pivot when needed.

items.paragraph:
Cultivating Confidence
Confidence is a necessary quality for both men and women in leadership. Yet due to the confidence gap, some women may have to work harder than their male counterparts to develop confidence in their careers. So how do we do that?

items.heading: Recognize Negative Patterns and Challenge Them
items.paragraph: The first step is becoming aware of negative thought patterns. Examples of these include:

back.description: Seeing situations in black-and-white terms, without acknowledging the gray areas or nuances.
Expecting the worst possible outcome, even when evidence suggests otherwise.
Drawing broad conclusions based on limited evidence, often leading to negative self-assessment.
Taking responsibility for events or outcomes that are beyond your control.
Focusing solely on the negative aspects of a situation while ignoring the positive elements.
Assuming you know what others are thinking, often attributing negative thoughts to them without evidence.
Setting rigid, unrealistic expectations for oneself and others, leading to constant feelings of inadequacy (e.g., “I should have finished that report sooner!”).

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Once you’ve learned how to limit negative thought patterns, the next step is replacing the negative thoughts with positive self-talk.

items.heading: Become a Master of Self-Talk
items.paragraph: Pat practiced self-talk with her players, especially in tight, important games. “Our attitude [was] ‘You couldn’t be better prepared. You know exactly what to do. So go do it,’” she recalls.
The power of self-talk is undeniable, influencing our thoughts, emotions, and ultimately, our actions. One key to being a master of positive self-talk is to practice affirmations regularly.

items.title: Daily Affirmations
items.description:
Affirmations are powerful statements that reinforce positive beliefs about oneself. To do this, create a list of affirmations tailored to your professional goals and repeat them regularly. For example:

 

I am right where I need to be in this moment.

I have enough time to do everything that is important to me.

I am strong, I am powerful, and I have everything I need.

I greet this day with gratitude.

I am more than up to the challenge.

I am at the peak of my career—and the best is yet to come!

items.title: Replace "I Can't" with "I Can"
items.description:
The language we use internally shapes our mindset and influences our actions. Swap limiting phrases like "I can't" with empowering alternatives like "I can" or "I will."

 

Instead of: “I can’t master pivot tables.”

Reframe: “I will master pivot tables in Excel!”

 

Instead of: “I can’t lead a meeting that confidently.”

Reframe: “I can lead a meeting that confidently, with some practice.”

items.title: Constructive Self-Criticism vs. Destructive Self-Talk
items.description: There's a fine line between constructive self-criticism and destructive self-talk. Instead of dwelling on mistakes with statements like, "I always mess up," or “I should have known better,” reframe your self-talk to focus on improvement: "I can learn from this and do better next time."

items.title: Celebrate Your Strengths
items.description: Women often downplay their achievements or attribute success to external factors. Shift your self-talk by consciously focusing on your strengths and celebrating your accomplishments. (“I know how to rock a speech and can do it again!”) Acknowledge the unique skills, talents, and value you bring to your team.

items.heading: Surround Yourself With Positive Influences
items.paragraph: Finally, the people we surround ourselves with significantly impact our mindset! Seek out positive influences and build a supportive network for your leadership career. Engage with colleagues, mentors, or friends specifically who uplift and encourage you. Share your goals and aspirations with those who genuinely celebrate your successes. By surrounding yourself with positivity, you create an environment that automatically reinforces constructive self-talk and bolsters your confidence.

items.heading: Deep Dive: The Three Types of Confidence
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

attachment.originalUrl: L6.2 Transcript Three Types of Confidence.pdf

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: OK, so we all know confidence is important to having success as a leader. But did you know that not all confidence is the same? There are three main types of confidence that you will encounter in your career:

back.description: Often characterized as "fake it till you make it,” isn’t all bad – it can be somewhat useful when starting a new challenge or career role. It involves leaning heavily on your past successes to navigate the unfamiliar territory until you can build confidence of your own in that area.

Conditional confidence means confidence that fluctuates based on external outcomes. When things are going well, you’re confident in that area! When things aren’t going well, doubt tends to creep in, and you feel insecure about your abilities. This type of confidence is a trap many people fall into during their careers.

Unconditional confidence is the end goal, where your confidence and overall self-assurance is largely rooted in the things you can control—your habits, effort, and attitude—rather than external factors. This stable, more resilient form of confidence is key to thriving as a leader in your career.
